decisive_facts.fact: The service runs as 4 gunicorn worker processes that share nothing, and each worker is recycled after about 2000 requests, starting with an empty cache.
The upstream registry API allows 60 metadata requests per hour per account and returns 429 for the rest of the hour once exceeded.
Every request handler needs metadata, so a 429 takes the whole service down until the hour resets.
Metadata changes a few times a day at most, so a long TTL is safe.

pros: No shared state to corrupt or lock
cons: Each of the 4 workers fetches every TLD itself: 4x the upstream calls
Every worker recycle (every ~2000 requests) restarts from cold and refetches; with a few dozen TLDs, two or three recycles in an hour exceed the 60/hour budget
No TTL: a worker that lives long serves stale metadata indefinitely

pros: One fetch per TLD per TTL for the whole host, independent of worker count and recycling
A TTL can be enforced in one place
cons: Needs atomic writes (write-then-rename) and a lock or single-flight so 4 workers do not all fetch on a miss
Disk read on every hit unless paired with a short in-process layer
Cache lives per host; multiple hosts still fetch separately

open_questions: How many hosts run this service? If more than one, the per-account budget is shared across hosts too and a shared file per host may still not be enough.
Is a stale read of up to an hour acceptable when metadata changes?
